point.title: American Lessons Learned about the War/ What was the war about?
point.partial_transcript: Oh, you have so many books. Have you read them all? Have you read them all?
point.synopsis: Conversation resumes with McMorris talking to An about books on the war, to which An answer and then that segues into conversation about him being a journalist. McMorris transitions the conversation by reflecting on his American perspective and what was learned from the Vietnam war. This includes bringing up Iraq and asking, “are we just making the same mistake over and over again?” This begins a long answer and subsequent conversation in which An details communist ideology as a way to explain American involvement under JFK. He proposes some lessons learned including a central one about the war being one of communist liberation. An provides a broad overview of the war beginning in 1945, explaining the motivations of various countries and their subsequent reactions and participation. They end by discussing the Vietnamese people and why they “joined the revolution.”

point.title: Vietnamese Nationalism, Ideologies, and Explanations for the War and U.S. Defeat
point.partial_transcript: But you said that not many of them knew about communism. They just wanted independence.
point.synopsis: They begin by discussing how many of the active Vietnamese participants during the war did not know about communism and, “just wanted independence, ” with an emphasizing social change, required independence first. They continue to talk, clarifying that according to An even soldiers, were fighting for independence and “ without independence we [the soldiers] don't think about socialism.” He comments that this is despite and perhaps because of limited levels of education and exposure to communist ideology. The conversation shifts when McMorris returns to the topic of America and what Americans, “still don't understand,” about “why we lost the war.” An then gives a long historical answer that includes outlining the importance of Karl Marx and the communist manifesto. He uses communism, capitalism, nationalism, dictatorship and American democracy to try and explain the many reasons America lost the war. An ends his long answer by stating the diplomat/historian Alexis de Tocqueville and the ways that Tocqueville's theories help explain American ideology the best.

point.title: From America’s Anti-Communism/Reasons for Involvement to China’s Political Power Structure
point.synopsis: Phan Xuan An, having established a detailed background, returns to the earlier discussion about why America got involved in war. This leads An to discuss Chinese politics including the tensions and history between Jiang Zemin, Hi Jintao, Deng Xiao Ping and Taiwan. The segment ends with a brief comment about China having a socialist system that is, “ a mechanism to control the masses,” but China also maintains capitalism.

point.title: Phạm Xuân Ẩn life philosophy and thoughts on fate
point.partial_transcript: Look at My Lai. Not all of them, like, behave like Mr. Calley.
point.synopsis: Phan Xuan An sits back down and they begin a brief discussion about the My Lai Massacre and its nuances and legacy. He shifts from talking about how hatred is conditioned to giving general musings about life, discussing how life is controlled a lot by fate. He tells a story about a former classmate who had a bright future, but her life became unhappy because her husband became addicted to drugs and their marriage failed. He uses this story to show that even educated and privileged people can suffer because of destiny. He briefly talks about his own life during the war. Many cadres and people were killed or captured, but he survived. He believes this was partly because of protection and fate; he mentions being protected by a “goddess.” He also speaks about Americans and reconciliation after the war. He suggests that ordinary people can get along despite past conflicts and that understanding between cultures is possible. Overall, he reflects on fate, survival, suffering, and the possibility of reconciliation after war.
point.keywords: Saigon; communist cadres; American people; Vietnamese culture; Vietnamese.; My Lai Massacre; fate; propaganda
